name: UK Resettlement Programmes — Local Authority Integration Funding 2025–2026
description: The UK government provides tariff-based funding to local authorities, healthcare providers, and community sponsors to support refugees resettled through UK Resettlement Programmes (including the UK Resettlement Scheme and Afghan schemes). Funding covers integration support for up to five years, including housing orientation, English language provision (ESOL), employment and skills training, healthcare registration, school enrolment for children, and community integration activities. Local authorities receive per-capita funding to deliver or commission these services for newly arrived refugees. The programme is administered by the Home Office with support from the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities. Refugees do not apply directly — support is provided through their local council upon arrival.
eligibility: Refugees resettled to the UK through official UK Resettlement Programmes (UK Resettlement Scheme, Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme, Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy); support delivered via the assigned local authority
amount: Per-capita tariff funding to local authorities — covers housing, ESOL, healthcare registration, and integration costs for up to 5 years
applicationProcess: Refugees do not apply directly. Upon resettlement to the UK through an official programme, the assigned local authority receives government funding to provide integration support. Contact your local council's resettlement team or the Home Office for information about services available in your area.
geographicScope: United Kingdom — all regions; delivered through participating local authorities across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland
documentsRequired: No direct application from refugees; local authorities access funding through Home Office grant claims. Refugees need their resettlement documentation and biometric residence permit (BRP).

name: ACH — Refugee Housing, Employment & Integration Services (UK)
description: ACH is a UK-based social enterprise founded in 2008 by Fuad Mahamed, himself a former refugee, to support newly arrived refugees and migrants in rebuilding their lives. Operating across Bristol, Birmingham, Coventry, Wolverhampton, and Solihull, ACH provides an integrated model of housing, employment training, and skills development. Services include safe and affordable housing for refugees, the Bridge to Employment programme offering job readiness training and sector-specific skills courses, enterprise support for those wanting to start businesses, ESOL and digital skills classes, sustainability training, and community integration activities. In 2025, ACH supported over 1,500 people with housing, learning, and employment opportunities. ACH also conducts research and advocacy on migrant equity in social housing, and publishes guidance for the wider housing sector on supporting refugees effectively.
eligibility: Refugees, asylum seekers, and migrants in the UK, particularly those in Bristol, Birmingham, Coventry, Wolverhampton, and Solihull; services are open regardless of nationality
amount: Free services — housing, employment training, skills development, and integration support provided at no cost to participants
applicationProcess: Contact ACH through their website (ach.org.uk) or visit one of their offices in Bristol, Birmingham, Coventry, Wolverhampton, or Solihull. Self-referrals and referrals from other agencies are accepted. An initial assessment identifies housing needs, employment goals, and appropriate programme placement. Participants receive tailored support plans combining housing, training, and integration activities.
geographicScope: United Kingdom — Bristol, Birmingham, Coventry, Wolverhampton, and Solihull (West Midlands and South West England)
documentsRequired: Proof of immigration status or asylum claim; identification documents; referral from a support agency is helpful but not required for self-referral

name: MOSAIC BC — Settlement & Integration Services for Newcomers (Canada)
description: MOSAIC is one of the largest settlement agencies in British Columbia, Canada, providing comprehensive services to immigrants, refugees, and migrant workers. Operating from 31 client-accessible sites across Greater Vancouver and the Fraser Valley, MOSAIC offers settlement assistance, English language training (LINC and EAL classes), employment programmes including job search support and sector-specific skills training, interpretation and translation services in over 30 languages, counselling and family services, legal information, victim services, and community outreach for families, children, youth, and seniors. The Settlement & Integration Programme includes conversation circles, youth groups, educational workshops on Canadian systems (healthcare, legal, housing, education), and community connections activities. Newcomers requiring more intensive support receive Guided Pathways case management. MOSAIC also operates specialized programmes for refugee claimants, temporary foreign workers, and women experiencing violence.
eligibility: Immigrants, refugees, refugee claimants, temporary residents, and migrant workers in British Columbia; most IRCC-funded settlement services require permanent residency or protected person status, but some MOSAIC programs serve all newcomers regardless of status
amount: Free — all settlement and integration services are provided at no cost; funded by IRCC and provincial/municipal grants
applicationProcess: Visit any of MOSAIC's 31 sites in Greater Vancouver and Fraser Valley, call their main office, or register online at mosaicbc.org. An intake worker will assess your settlement needs and connect you with appropriate programmes — language training, employment support, counselling, legal information, or community integration activities. Walk-ins are welcome at most locations.
geographicScope: Canada — Greater Vancouver and Fraser Valley, British Columbia; some online programmes available province-wide
documentsRequired: Immigration documents (confirmation of permanent residence, refugee claim, work permit, or other status); government-issued ID; additional documents may be needed for specific programmes (e.g. language assessment for LINC classes)

name: Canada IRCC Settlement Program — Free Newcomer Services Nationwide
description: The Government of Canada invests approximately $1.2 billion annually in settlement services to help newcomers integrate into Canadian life. Through the IRCC Settlement Program, over 500 service provider organizations across the country (outside Quebec) deliver free services including needs assessment and referrals, language training (LINC — Language Instruction for Newcomers to Canada), employment-related services such as job search workshops and credential recognition support, community connections to help newcomers build social networks, and support services such as transportation, childcare, translation, and disability support to ensure programmes are accessible. As of April 2026, economic immigrants can access these services for up to six years after obtaining permanent residence. A new Equity Stream launched in 2025 provides additional funding to grassroots organizations serving equity-deserving newcomer populations. Services are delivered in multiple languages across all provinces and territories except Quebec, which operates its own settlement programme.
eligibility: Permanent residents, protected persons (Convention refugees and persons in need of protection), and individuals approved for permanent residence in Canada; economic immigrants eligible for up to 6 years after obtaining PR (as of April 2026); Quebec residents access separate provincial services
amount: Free — approximately $1.2 billion in federal funding supports free settlement services nationwide; includes transportation, childcare, and translation support
applicationProcess: Use the IRCC 'Find free newcomer services near you' tool at ircc.canada.ca to locate settlement organizations in your area. Visit or contact your local service provider to complete a needs assessment. You will be connected with appropriate services including language classes, employment support, and community integration programmes. No separate application to IRCC is needed — services are accessed directly through local providers.
geographicScope: Canada — all provinces and territories except Quebec (which operates its own programme); over 500 service providers in more than 3,000 locations
documentsRequired: Confirmation of Permanent Residence (CoPR) or Protected Person status documentation; government-issued ID; specific programmes may require additional documents (e.g. language assessment placement test for LINC)

name: ORR Refugee Support Services (RSS) — Employment, Childcare & Transportation Assistance
organization: Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
description: The Refugee Support Services (RSS) programme, administered by the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), provides employment-focused assistance to help refugees and other eligible populations achieve economic self-sufficiency in the United States. RSS funds are distributed to states and replacement designees to deliver employment services, vocational training, on-the-job training, English language instruction, and case management. Critically, RSS also covers support services that remove barriers to employment, including transportation assistance (bus passes, ride-sharing stipends, driver's education), childcare subsidies for parents attending training or working, and translation or interpretation during job placement. Individuals are eligible for RSS for up to five years from their date of eligibility. The programme complements Refugee Cash Assistance (RCA) and Refugee Medical Assistance (RMA) by addressing the practical barriers — such as lack of transportation or childcare — that prevent refugees from entering and sustaining employment.
eligibility: Refugees, asylees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, Special Immigrant Visa holders, certified victims of trafficking, and Amerasians; eligible for up to 5 years from date of eligibility (date of arrival, asylum grant, or certification)
amount: Free services — employment training, transportation assistance (bus passes, ride subsidies), childcare subsidies, English classes, and job placement support provided at no cost
applicationProcess: Contact your local resettlement agency or state refugee coordinator. Upon arrival or status determination, refugees are connected to a local service provider who conducts an employment assessment and develops an individual self-sufficiency plan. Services including job training, transportation assistance, childcare, and English classes are arranged based on needs. Visit acf.gov/orr for a directory of state refugee coordinators and local service providers.
geographicScope: United States — nationwide; administered through state refugee programmes and local resettlement agencies in all 50 states and the District of Columbia
documentsRequired: Proof of eligible immigration status (I-94, I-571, asylum approval letter, SIV documentation, or trafficking certification); Social Security card or application receipt; state-issued ID or immigration documents

name: ORR Refugee Family Child Care Microenterprise Development (RFCCMED)
organization: Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
description: The Refugee Family Child Care Microenterprise Development (RFCCMED) programme is a specialised ORR initiative that helps refugees start licensed family childcare businesses in their own homes. The programme addresses two critical needs simultaneously: it provides refugee parents with a pathway to economic self-sufficiency through entrepreneurship, and it increases the availability of culturally and linguistically appropriate childcare in refugee communities. RFCCMED grantees provide participants with training on child development, health and safety, business management, and state licensing requirements. They also offer direct financial assistance to help prepare homes for childcare operations (safety modifications, equipment, supplies), and ongoing technical assistance through the licensing process and first year of business operation. The programme operates through competitively selected grantee organisations across the United States and has helped hundreds of refugees establish sustainable childcare businesses while serving their communities.
eligibility: Refugees, asylees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, Special Immigrant Visa holders, certified victims of trafficking, and Amerasians who are interested in starting a family childcare business; must be within ORR eligibility period; must be willing to pursue state childcare licensing
amount: Training, licensing support, and direct financial assistance for home preparation — amounts vary by grantee organization; covers safety modifications, equipment, supplies, and business startup costs
applicationProcess: Contact your local resettlement agency or state refugee coordinator to find out if an RFCCMED grantee operates in your area. Interested participants undergo an intake assessment and orientation. The programme includes training modules on child development, health/safety, business management, and state licensing. Financial assistance for home modifications and equipment is provided after completing training milestones. Technical support continues through the licensing process and into the first year of operation.
geographicScope: United States — available in select metropolitan areas through competitively awarded ORR grants; check acf.gov/orr/grants for current grantee locations
documentsRequired: Proof of eligible immigration status; government-issued ID; proof of residence suitable for home-based childcare; willingness to undergo background checks required for childcare licensing
